# Model composition and structured populations

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 2, Session 2. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

Complex epidemic models are easier to audit when they are assembled from
named components. A force-of-infection component can be connected to
susceptible and infectious components, or a reaction network can be reused as
an ODE, chemical-Langevin SDE, or jump process. This appendix shows both
patterns with current `ModelingToolkit.jl` 11 and `Catalyst.jl` 16 APIs.

## Learning goals

By the end of this appendix you should be able to:

- compose symbolic `System` components and compile their connections with
  `mtkcompile`;
- represent a two-group population as a reaction network with explicit
  cross-group infections; and
- turn one Catalyst model into deterministic, diffusion, and jump problem
  types while keeping assumptions visible.

## Model assumptions and classification

The first example is a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state SIR
model assembled from three symbolic components. The components share the
population variables through explicit connection equations.

The second example is a deterministic/stochastic comparison for a structured
population with two groups. It is a continuous-time model with discrete
population states for the jump process and continuous states for its ODE and
chemical-Langevin approximations. Each group has `S_k`, `I_k`, and `R_k`.
Within-group contact rates are `c_1 = c_2 = 10`; cross-group contact
multipliers are `m_{12} = m_{21} = 0.5`. Each group starts with 500 people,
five of whom are infectious. These cross-group factors are an intentional
departure from homogeneous mixing.

## Equations

For the component example, the connections reduce to the standard equations

$$
\dot S = -\beta\frac{SI}{N},\qquad
\dot I = \beta\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\qquad
\dot R = \gamma I,\qquad N=S+I+R.
\tag{6}
$$ {#eq-a09-composed-sir}

For two groups, the infection flow into group 1 is

$$
\lambda_1 =
\frac{\beta c_1}{N}\left(S_1 I_1 + m_{12}S_1 I_2\right),
\tag{7}
$$ {#eq-a09-group1}

and the analogous flow into group 2 is

$$
\lambda_2 =
\frac{\beta c_2}{N}\left(m_{21}S_2 I_1 + S_2 I_2\right).
\tag{8}
$$ {#eq-a09-group2}

Thus `S₁` loses individuals through the first two infection reactions, `I₁`
gains those individuals and loses them at rate `γI₁`, and `R₁` gains the
recoveries. Group 2 follows the same pattern. A reaction network stores these
flows as stoichiometric changes plus propensity expressions; Catalyst then
generates the problem-specific equations.

## Julia implementation

### Composing symbolic SIR components

ModelingToolkit 11's current composition documentation uses `System`,
`compose`, and `mtkcompile`. The component constructors below deliberately
keep the equations separate. The top-level connection system says which
symbols refer to the same biological state and forwards the shared parameters.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie
using Catalyst
using JumpProcesses
using ModelingToolkit
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random
using StochasticDiffEq
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D

@variables S(t) I(t) R(t)
@parameters β γ

@named susceptible_component = System(
    [D(S) ~ -β * S * I / (S + I + R)],
    t,
)
@named infectious_component = System(
    [D(I) ~ β * S * I / (S + I + R) - γ * I],
    t,
)
@named recovered_component = System([D(R) ~ γ * I], t)

sir_composed = compose(
    System(
        [
            S ~ infectious_component.S,
            I ~ susceptible_component.I,
            R ~ infectious_component.R,
            infectious_component.S ~ susceptible_component.S,
            susceptible_component.I ~ infectious_component.I,
            susceptible_component.R ~ recovered_component.R,
            infectious_component.R ~ recovered_component.R,
            recovered_component.I ~ infectious_component.I,
        ],
        t,
        [S, I, R],
        [β, γ],
        bindings = [
            susceptible_component.β => β,
            infectious_component.β => β,
            infectious_component.γ => γ,
            recovered_component.γ => γ,
        ],
        name = :sir,
    ),
    susceptible_component,
    infectious_component,
    recovered_component,
)

compiled_sir = mtkcompile(sir_composed)
nothing
```

`mtkcompile` removes the algebraic forwarding equations and returns the
three-state system in @eq-a09-composed-sir. The current problem constructor
accepts a single dictionary containing both initial values and parameters.

```{julia}
component_problem = ODEProblem(
    compiled_sir,
    Dict(
        susceptible_component.S => 990.0,
        infectious_component.I => 10.0,
        recovered_component.R => 0.0,
        β => 0.05,
        γ => 0.25,
    ),
    (0.0, 10.0),
)
component_solution = solve(component_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1)
```

### One structured reaction network, three problem types

The Catalyst DSL makes the two-group assumptions explicit. The denominator
parameter `N` keeps the mass-action propensities on the same per-capita scale
as the baseline SIR model. The same `ReactionSystem` is passed directly to
the current `ODEProblem`, `SDEProblem`, and `JumpProblem` constructors.

```{julia}
two_group_network = @reaction_network begin
    @parameters N
    (β * c1) / N, S1 + I1 --> 2I1
    (β * c1 * m12) / N, S1 + I2 --> I1 + I2
    (β * c2 * m21) / N, S2 + I1 --> I2 + I1
    (β * c2) / N, S2 + I2 --> 2I2
    γ, I1 --> R1
    γ, I2 --> R2
end

group_initial_values = [
    :S1 => 495.0, :I1 => 5.0, :R1 => 0.0,
    :S2 => 495.0, :I2 => 5.0, :R2 => 0.0,
]
group_parameters = [
    :N => 1000.0,
    :β => 0.05,
    :c1 => 10.0,
    :c2 => 10.0,
    :m12 => 0.5,
    :m21 => 0.5,
    :γ => 0.25,
]
group_tspan = (0.0, 2.0)
group_saveat = 0.05

ode_problem = ODEProblem(
    two_group_network,
    group_initial_values,
    group_tspan,
    group_parameters,
)
ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = group_saveat)

Random.seed!(20260711)
sde_problem = SDEProblem(
    two_group_network,
    group_initial_values,
    group_tspan,
    group_parameters,
)
sde_solution = solve(
    sde_problem,
    LambaEM();
    dt = 0.01,
    saveat = group_saveat,
)

Random.seed!(20260712)
jump_problem = JumpProblem(
    two_group_network,
    [
        :S1 => 495, :I1 => 5, :R1 => 0,
        :S2 => 495, :I2 => 5, :R2 => 0,
    ],
    group_tspan,
    group_parameters,
)
jump_solution = solve(jump_problem; saveat = group_saveat)
```

The ODE and SDE use continuous-valued states. The jump model uses integer
counts and Gillespie-style event times. `LambaEM` is the current
`StochasticDiffEq` Euler--Maruyama algorithm name used for a
chemical-Langevin approximation; its noise can leave the nonnegative domain
when populations are small, which is discussed below.

### Comparing aggregate infectious prevalence

```{julia}
#| label: fig-a09-composition
#| fig-cap: "Aggregate infectious prevalence from a composed ODE, chemical-Langevin SDE, and jump realization."
ode_infected = ode_solution[:I1] .+ ode_solution[:I2]
sde_infected = sde_solution[:I1] .+ sde_solution[:I2]
jump_infected = jump_solution[:I1] .+ jump_solution[:I2]

fig = Figure(size = (850, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious individuals")
lines!(ax, ode_solution.t, ode_infected; color = :black, linewidth = 3, label = "ODE")
lines!(ax, sde_solution.t, sde_infected; color = :darkorange, linewidth = 2, label = "SDE")
stairs!(ax, jump_solution.t, jump_infected; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "Jump")
axislegend(ax; position = :lt)
fig
```

## Validation

The reaction stoichiometry should conserve the total population in every
trajectory (the diffusion approximation is checked separately because
floating-point noise can be large). We also check that the composed
deterministic model has the expected three equations after compilation.

```{julia}
component_equation_count = length(equations(compiled_sir))
ode_population = ode_solution[:S1] .+ ode_solution[:I1] .+ ode_solution[:R1] .+
    ode_solution[:S2] .+ ode_solution[:I2] .+ ode_solution[:R2]
jump_population = jump_solution[:S1] .+ jump_solution[:I1] .+ jump_solution[:R1] .+
    jump_solution[:S2] .+ jump_solution[:I2] .+ jump_solution[:R2]
ode_population_error = maximum(abs.(ode_population .- 1000.0))
jump_population_error = maximum(abs.(jump_population .- 1000))
(;
    component_equation_count,
    ode_population_error,
    jump_population_error,
    sde_minimum_state = minimum(Array(sde_solution)),
)
```

The deterministic and jump population errors should be near zero. The SDE
minimum is reported rather than silently clipped; a negative value is a
diagnostic of using an unconstrained Gaussian diffusion for count data, not a
biological prediction.

## Interpretation and limitations

Composition makes assumptions inspectable: connections are named, parameters
are forwarded explicitly, and the compiled equations can be checked before
simulation. A reaction network gives a second kind of reuse: the same
stoichiometric model can support a mean-field ODE, a chemical-Langevin SDE,
and an exact-event jump process. This is useful for comparing approximation
error, not for assuming that the three trajectories are interchangeable.

Two-group mixing is only one structured-population choice. Age structure,
spatial movement, births, waning immunity, and contact networks require
additional states and reactions. A chemical-Langevin SDE is most defensible
when propensities are sufficiently large; it does not enforce integer counts
or positivity. The jump model is discrete and stochastic, so one realization
is not a replacement for an ensemble or uncertainty interval.

The current [ModelingToolkit composition guide](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/basics/Composition/)
documents `System`, `compose`, and `mtkcompile`. The
[Catalyst documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/Catalyst/stable/) documents
the DSL and direct construction of ODE, SDE, and jump problems. For a primary
software reference, see [Loman et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011530).
The structured mixing idea follows the contact-pattern formulation of
Jacquez et al. [@jacquez1988].

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#a09-ex1}

Add a third population group with its own contact rate and two cross-group
mixing multipliers. Keep the total population at 1000, construct the network
with the Catalyst DSL, and verify conservation for both an ODE solve and a
jump realization. Compare the aggregate infectious curve with the two-group
model and state which new parameters are identifiable from aggregate
incidence alone.

### Exercise 2 {#a09-ex2}

Use the same reaction network to run at least 100 jump realizations with a
deterministic seed sequence. Plot the mean and a pointwise 90% interval for
aggregate infectious prevalence, and compare the mean with the ODE trajectory.
Explain why the SDE curve need not lie inside that interval and how the
choice of `N` and initial counts affects the approximation.
